meaning: The speed at which someone walks, runs or moves; also the speed at which something happens
trick: PACE = the SPACE you cover per second, without the S.
examples: He was swinging his big felt hat, trying to make the pace.
She walked at a fast pace to catch the bus.

usage.pattern: at a + fast/slow/steady pace / keep up the pace

meaning: Walked back and forth again and again, usually because worried or restless
trick: PACED = took many PACES up and down the same floor.
examples: At first, Nana paced around the hut, clenching and unclenching her fists.
He paced the room while waiting for the results.

meaning: Single steps, or the distance covered by a step
trick: PACES = steps you count while PACING.
examples: My mom stood several paces behind him.
The dog stopped a few paces from the door.

meaning: Walking back and forth again and again, often because of worry, anger or impatience
trick: PACING = a tiger PACING in its cage.
examples: Mammy was pacing and ranting while Babi sat quietly, waiting for the storm to pass.
He kept pacing the hall outside the exam room.

meaning: A group of people or animals, often said with disapproval; also a set of things wrapped together
trick: PACK of wolves = a group that moves together.
examples: Everything they did was for their own benefit, not for a pack of idle, thieving human beings.
A pack of wild dogs ran across the field.

meaning: Filled or covered with soft material for comfort or protection
trick: PADDED = has a PAD inside, like a cricket pad.
examples: The padded headpiece felt tight and heavy on her head.
She bought a padded jacket for the winter.

meaning: Flooded fields where rice is grown
trick: PADDY = rice field; PADDIES = many of them (like Hindi 'dhaan').
examples: Babi pointed to rice paddies and barley fields covering the slopes.
Farmers were planting rice in the paddies.

usage.pattern: rice paddies / work in the paddies

meaning: A small fenced field where horses or other animals are kept or grazed
trick: PADDOCK = a field with a lock (fence) where horses PAD about.
examples: The two of them spent their Sundays in the small paddock beyond the orchard, grazing side by side.
The horses were let out into the paddock.

usage.pattern: in the paddock / a paddock for + animals

meaning: Belonging to old religions with many gods, not one of the main world religions
trick: PAGAN = PAGe from ANcient times, before the big religions.
examples: One bad value is sacrificing small animals to the pagan gods.
The festival has its roots in an old pagan ritual.

meaning: A bucket, usually with a handle
trick: PAIL = PAIL of water; Jack and Jill fetched a pail.
examples: She drew a pail of water from the well and washed the windows.
He carried a pail of milk from the barn.

meaning: Showing that someone is hurt, upset or in pain
trick: PAINED = filled with PAIN.
examples: She lowered herself onto the chair with a pained sigh.
He gave me a pained look when I laughed at him.

meaning: The top inside part of the mouth; also a person's sense of taste
trick: PALATE is on the roof of the mouth; PLATE holds the food it tastes.
examples: It was the first time she'd eaten ice cream; she never imagined such tricks could be played on a palate.
This spicy curry may be too strong for a young child's palate.

meaning: Long, unnecessary talk or discussion, often to settle something
trick: PALAVERING = PALAVER = a big chat-fest that goes on and on.
examples: After some palavering among the judge, the prosecutor and my lawyer, the court took a break.
After an hour of palavering, the committee finally agreed.

usage.pattern: after some palavering / palavering about something

meaning: Light in colour, not bright; also, in the idiom 'beyond the ...', totally unacceptable
trick: PALE = PALE face when you see a ghost; 'beyond the pale' = outside the fence of decency.
examples: Overhead, clouds slid past a pale moon.
She looked pale after the long illness.

usage.pattern: look/turn pale / a pale + colour/noun / beyond the pale

meaning: From the early Stone Age; also (humorous) extremely old or long
trick: PALEO (old) + LITH (stone) = Old Stone Age.
examples: Seconds on the biology clock now feel like Paleolithic eons.
Paleolithic people made tools from stone.

meaning: A dark, heavy feeling or cloud that covers something; also a thick cloud of smoke
trick: PALL = a heavy cloth (pall) thrown over everyone's mood.
examples: A pall of shame and grief fell over Laila.
The bad news cast a pall over the party.

usage.pattern: cast a pall over something / a pall of + smoke/gloom

meaning: Pale and unhealthy-looking; also lacking life or colour
trick: PALLID = PALE + sickly; a pallid face looks ill.
examples: Mammy's heart was like a pallid beach where Laila's footprints would forever wash away.
He looked pallid after a week in bed.

meaning: An unhealthy pale colour of the face or skin
trick: PALLOR = the PALE colour of an ill person.
examples: His scarlet ears stood out like blobs of sealing wax on the pallor of his cheeks.
Her pallor told us she was not well.

meaning: Thick dark clouds of smoke or dust
trick: PALLS = dark covers (palls) of smoke over a city.
examples: Fires raged, and black palls of smoke mushroomed over snow-covered buildings.
After the factory fire, black palls of smoke hung over the town.

meaning: So strong or clear that it can almost be felt or touched
trick: PALPABLE = you can PALP (touch) it, like a PALM touching it.
examples: Even though we were one of few black families in town, I didn't feel any palpable racism.
The tension in the room was palpable.

meaning: Fast, strong or uneven heartbeats that a person can feel
hindi: धड़कन तेज़ होना, दिल की धड़कन
trick: PALPITATIONS = heart going PAL-PIT-PAL-PIT very fast.
examples: That leads to swelling in the feet, heart palpitations and shortness of breath.
Too much coffee gives me palpitations.

meaning: Acting or speaking insincerely, dodging the truth or haggling unfairly
trick: PALTERING = PALTRY tricks: playing games instead of being honest.
examples: He hoped justice would be done without paltering.
The minister answered without paltering, and everyone respected that.

usage.pattern: without paltering / paltering with the truth

meaning: Small thin booklets with information about one subject
trick: PAMPHLETS = PAM handed out thin LETS-read booklets.
examples: Mammy showed her the old newspaper clippings and pamphlets that Ahmad had collected.
Volunteers handed out pamphlets about road safety.

usage.pattern: hand out / distribute pamphlets about something

meaning: A light hat made of fine straw, worn in hot weather
trick: PANAMA HAT: a straw hat famous from the PANAMA Canal workers.
examples: He leaned forward, elbows on knees and his Panama hat between his hands.
Grandpa wears a Panama hat in the summer sun.

meaning: A sudden sharp pain or strong feeling
trick: PANG = a sudden BANG of pain.
examples: She felt that first, tremendous pang of pain.
She felt a pang of guilt when she saw his face.

meaning: A small metal cup or pan (mostly British, old-fashioned)
trick: PANNIKIN = a mini PAN, a 'pan-kin' (little pan).
examples: After the jailer left me I shined up my tin pannikin and studied my face in it.
He drank his tea from a tin pannikin.

usage.pattern: a tin pannikin / a pannikin of + drink

meaning: Breathing quickly and loudly, usually after running or effort
trick: PANTING = a dog PANTS with its tongue out.
examples: She ran up then down the street, panting, near tears now.
The dog lay panting in the shade.

meaning: Showed someone or something to others in order to impress or be chosen; also marched in a procession
trick: PARADED = put on PARADE, like soldiers shown to the crowd.
examples: One by one, the women paraded the neighborhood girls who might be suitable brides.
The winning team paraded the trophy through the streets.

meaning: In a way that seems strange or opposite to what you expect
hindi: विरोधाभासी रूप से, अजीब तरह से
trick: PARADOX = two opposites (PARA + DOX) true together.
examples: And, paradoxically, accepting a negative experience is itself a positive experience.
Paradoxically, the more tired I am, the harder it is to sleep.

meaning: An oil fuel burned in lamps and heaters (British word for kerosene); also a soft white wax
trick: PARAFFIN lamp = PARA-FIRE lamp that burns oil.
examples: He began by lighting a paraffin lamp.
Grandma kept a paraffin lamp for power cuts.

meaning: A small, colourful bird of the parrot family with a long tail
trick: PARAKEET = PARrot's little KEEt-sized cousin.
examples: The suitor had been a boy from Shindand, a young parakeet seller.
Our green parakeet can say a few words.

usage.pattern: a pet parakeet / a parakeet seller

meaning: Trained workers who give emergency medical help, usually in an ambulance
trick: PARAMEDICS = PARA (beside) + MEDICS: they help beside doctors.
examples: The paramedics arrived at the lake within minutes.
The paramedics took the injured man to hospital.

usage.pattern: paramedics arrive / be treated by paramedics

meaning: A strong, often unreasonable fear or suspicion that something bad will happen or that people are against you
trick: PARANOIA = feeling everyone is out to get you.
examples: There is no rush like the surge of adrenaline and paranoia that comes with falling from high altitude.
His paranoia made him check the locks again and again.

meaning: Too suspicious or fearful, believing others want to harm you
trick: PARANOID = a PARANOIA-filled person.
examples: My father was paranoid.
Don't be so paranoid; nobody is following you.

meaning: Living off others without giving anything back, like a parasite
trick: PARASITICAL = acting like a PARASITE (a tick on a dog).
examples: With the worthless parasitical human beings gone, there was more for everyone to eat.
He called the lazy officials a parasitical class.

meaning: Very dry because of no rain or heat; also very thirsty
trick: PARCHED = PARCH-ment dry, like dried paper.
examples: She was here now, over those boulders and parched hills, with a home of her own.
After the long walk, I was parched.

meaning: Thick paper made from animal skin, used long ago for writing
trick: PARCHMENT = PARCHED dry skin used as paper.
examples: The parchment on which Mammy meant to ink their legends.
The old map was drawn on parchment.

usage.pattern: written on parchment / a roll of parchment

meaning: A person who is rejected and avoided by others
trick: PARIAH sounds like 'PARE-ya': PARED off and pushed out of the group.
examples: The willingness to be different, an outcast, a pariah, all for your own values.
After the scandal he became a pariah in his village.

meaning: Stopped a vehicle and left it somewhere for a time
trick: PARKED = left the car in the PARK-ing.
examples: My mom parked, ducked under the tape, and I followed her to the front door.
He parked his bike outside the shop.

meaning: The crime of killing one's own father, mother or close relative
trick: PARRICIDE = PAR(ent) + CIDE (kill), like homicide.
examples: I expect you've heard about it; it's a case of parricide.
The court heard a rare case of parricide.

usage.pattern: a case of parricide / be accused of parricide

meaning: To repeat someone's words without thinking or understanding; also a talking bird
trick: PARROT = repeat like a PARROT (tota ratt).
examples: I didn't just parrot the Navy's script.
Students should not just parrot the textbook.

meaning: Divided or moved apart so there is a gap; also combed hair into two sides
trick: PARTED = made two PARTS.
examples: A gust of wind parted the drooping branches of the willow like a curtain.
The crowd parted to let the ambulance through.

meaning: Liking something very much (used with 'to'); also not complete
trick: PARTIAL TO = your heart takes its PART.
examples: As I am very partial to milky coffee, I said, "Thanks."
My dad is partial to a cup of tea after dinner.

meaning: More than usual; especially
hindi: ख़ास तौर पर, विशेष रूप से
trick: PARTICULARLY = this PARTICULAR one, more than others.
examples: For this son the king had a particularly grand idea.
It was particularly cold this morning.

meaning: Medium-sized brown wild birds, hunted or sold for food
trick: PARTRIDGE in a pear tree (Christmas song).
examples: She spotted him coming out of tiny booths that sold partridges.
We saw two partridges running through the field.

meaning: People who happen to be walking past a place
trick: PASSERSBY = those who PASS BY (plural on 'passers').
examples: Merchants peered out to sell textiles and fur coats to passersby.
The street singer smiled at passersby.

meaning: Of a soft, pale, light colour
trick: PASTEL = PASTE-like soft colours (baby pink, light blue).
examples: My brother and I were well dressed in jeans and pastel shirts.
She painted her room in pastel colours.

meaning: Something you do regularly for fun in your free time
trick: PASTIME = something to PASS the TIME.
examples: In Hawaii, bow hunting for wild pig in the mountains is a major pastime.
Reading is my favourite pastime.

meaning: Christian priests or ministers in charge of a church
trick: PASTORS = PASTURE keepers: shepherds of their church 'flock'.
examples: Pastors and ministers told their congregations that they were each special in God's eyes.
The two pastors led the Sunday prayers together.

meaning: Land covered with grass where farm animals feed
trick: PASTURE = where cows go PAST to eat grass.
examples: They all raced out into the pasture together.
The cows were grazing in the green pasture.

usage.pattern: in the pasture / put animals out to pasture

meaning: Ready and quick, as if prepared beforehand; also a light touch with the hand
trick: PAT answer = came out PAT-PAT, already ready.
examples: The answer came so pat that he seemed to be expecting my question.
Her excuse sounded too pat to be true.

meaning: A small area of something that is different from what is around it; also a piece of cloth sewn over a hole
trick: PATCH = a small PATCH of colour, like a cloth patch on jeans.
examples: The three of them sat outside the hut, in a patch of shade thrown by the willows.
There was a wet patch on the floor.

meaning: The small bone at the front of the knee (medical word)
hindi: घुटने की हड्डी, घुटने की टोपी
trick: PATELLA = little PAT on your knee - the kneecap.
examples: My patella was intact, but both of my shins had small fractures.
The doctor said the patella was not broken.

meaning: Made of leather with a very shiny, glossy surface
trick: PATENT-LEATHER = leather so shiny you could see your face.
examples: A little girl came by with a big pink bow and black patent-leather shoes.
He wore patent-leather shoes to the wedding.

meaning: Treating someone as if they are less clever or important than you
trick: PATRONIZING = acting like a big PATRON helping a 'poor little' person.
examples: That sweet gift she gave us is now remembered as patronizing and condescending.
Please don't be patronizing; I can do it myself.

meaning: Customers of a shop, restaurant or hotel; also people who support an art or cause
trick: PATRONS = people who PAT the shop with their money.
examples: One group of waiters praised and encouraged patrons with words like "great" and "sure."
The cafe offers free tea to its regular patrons.

meaning: A large, fat stomach (usually a man's)
trick: PAUNCH = a PUNCH-bag belly.
examples: Celeste was in his usual place, his apron bulging on his paunch.
My uncle's paunch grew after he stopped walking.

meaning: Covered with a hard surface like stone, bricks or concrete
trick: PAVED road = a PAVEMENT-like hard road.
examples: There were more cars, taller buildings and more paved roads.
The village finally got a paved road.

meaning: A path beside a road for people to walk on (British); also a road surface
trick: PAVEMENT = PAVED path for walking.
examples: The tobacconist brought a chair out on to the pavement and sat astride it.
Kids drew pictures with chalk on the pavement.

meaning: Flat stones or blocks that cover the ground; a paved surface
trick: PAVING stones = what you PAVE the path with.
examples: Though it was a fine afternoon, the paving blocks were black and glistening.
The paving outside the house is cracked.

meaning: Something left with a lender as a promise for a loan; also a less important piece in chess
trick: PAWN shop = leave your gold, get money; chess PAWN = small piece.
examples: Another time, he found a pawn ticket for two bracelets he'd never seen.
She had to put her watch in pawn to pay the rent.

usage.pattern: a pawn ticket / in pawn / pawn something

meaning: A shop that lends money to people who leave valuable items as a promise of repayment
trick: PAWNSHOP = shop where you PAWN (girvi) your things.
examples: They would fetch a taxi and take it all to a pawnshop.
He sold his old guitar to a pawnshop.

meaning: The feet of animals such as dogs and cats
trick: PAWS = cat's PAWS leave prints.
examples: There was a sound of boots and paws on the wooden stairs.
The puppy left muddy paws on the floor.

meaning: A sweet juicy fruit, narrow at the top and wide at the bottom
trick: PEAR looks like a PAIR of balls stuck together.
examples: It was the one of them sitting back-to-back under the pear tree.
I had a ripe pear for breakfast.

usage.pattern: a pear tree / a ripe pear

meaning: Formed small drops like pearls
trick: PEARLED = water made PEARLS on the skin.
examples: Water pearled on my scalp and dripped down my nose.
Sweat pearled on his forehead in the heat.

meaning: Poor farmers or farm workers who own little land, especially in the past
trick: PEASANTS = growing PEAS on their small farms.
examples: The photos showed young soldiers shaking hands with peasants.
In old times, peasants worked the land of the rich.

usage.pattern: poor peasants / peasants work the land

meaning: A small smooth round stone, often found on beaches and riverbeds
trick: PEBBLE = a PEA-sized stone in a BUBBLE of water.
examples: She didn't tell the girl that she'd once named a pebble after her.
The child threw a pebble into the pond.

meaning: Rude slang for a penis; also (old British idiom 'keep your ... up') courage, good spirits
trick: PECKER = something that PECKS, like a woodpecker; avoid in polite talk.
examples: The doctor told the boy that pecker is a rude word.
"Keep your pecker up!" my British grandmother said, meaning stay cheerful.

usage.pattern: someone's pecker / keep your pecker up (British, old)

meaning: Strange or unusual; also belonging only to one place or person
trick: PECULIAR = PECULIAR people are a little odd.
examples: And the behaviour of the cat was somewhat peculiar.
There's a peculiar smell in the kitchen.

usage.pattern: something is peculiar / peculiar to someone/something

meaning: To sell goods by going from place to place or calling to people; also to spread ideas
trick: PEDDLE = PEDAL your bike from street to street to sell.
examples: Merchants leaned out of the shadows now and then to peddle textiles and fur coats.
He peddles vegetables from a cart.

meaning: People walking in the street, not in a vehicle
trick: PEDESTRIANS = PED (foot) people, like PEDal.
examples: Mariam walked along crowded boulevards, amid a steady stream of pedestrians and bicycle riders.
The road has a bridge for pedestrians.

meaning: Removing something layer by layer, slowly uncovering what is underneath
trick: PEELING AWAY = like PEELING an onion, layer by layer.
examples: People who cheat must start peeling away at their self-awareness onion.
She began peeling away the old wallpaper.

meaning: Looked carefully or with difficulty at something
trick: PEERED = looked like a PEER (person) squinting.
examples: Animals tall enough peered in at the dining-room window.
She peered through the fog to find the road.

meaning: Looking carefully or with difficulty at something
hindi: झाँकते हुए, ग़ौर से देखते हुए
trick: PEERING = PEEKING but longer.
examples: There are people peering over the instructors' shoulders.
The kids were peering into the box.

meaning: Small hard balls, especially of lead fired from a gun; also small balls of food or other material
trick: PELLETS = tiny PELLETS pelting from a shotgun.
examples: The pellets buried themselves in the wall of the barn and the meeting broke up.
The farmer fed the rabbits food pellets.

meaning: Throwing many things at someone quickly; also (of rain) falling heavily
trick: PELTING = PELTing them with PELLETS.
examples: They took turns poking each other, giggling, pelting each other with bread crumbs.
Kids were pelting each other with snowballs.

usage.pattern: pelting someone with something / pelting rain

meaning: Something you do to show you are sorry for doing wrong
trick: PENANCE = PENalty you do to show you're sorry.
examples: They were halfhearted tokens of penance, insincere gestures.
He cleaned the whole house as penance for forgetting her birthday.

usage.pattern: do penance / as penance for something

meaning: A piece of jewellery hanging from a chain around the neck
trick: PENDANT = it hangs (PEND), like a PENDulum.
examples: Mariam opened the box and found a leaf-shaped pendant.
She wore a gold pendant on a thin chain.

usage.pattern: wear a pendant / a + gold/silver pendant

meaning: Hanging down loosely
trick: PENDULOUS = hanging and swinging like a PENDULUM.
examples: What caught my attention most was his pendulous, scarlet ears.
The tree had pendulous branches full of fruit.

meaning: Went into or through something; also was felt deeply
trick: PENETRATED = a PEN that went through the paper.
examples: The deep bass thud of machine-gun fire penetrated our guts.
Sunlight penetrated the thick curtains.

meaning: Seeming to see right into someone's thoughts; also sharp and loud
trick: PENETRATING eyes = eyes that go through you like a PEN.
examples: Even with the burqa between them, Laila was not protected from his penetrating eyes.
She gave me a penetrating look.

meaning: Plural of the male sex organ
trick: PENISES = plural of PENIS (medical word).
examples: The biology book had simple diagrams of penises and other body parts.
The old Greek statues have small penises, which made the kids giggle.

meaning: Shut in a small space; also wrote something
trick: PENNED in = locked in a PEN (animal enclosure).
examples: Here, anyhow, I wasn't penned in a hollow tree trunk.
The sheep were penned in for the night.

meaning: Small coins of low value (cents in the US)
trick: PENNIES = a PENNY each; save your pennies.
examples: We had two jars filled with pennies and other loose change.
She saved her pennies in a piggy bank.

usage.pattern: save pennies / a jar of pennies

meaning: Quietly thinking about something, often in a slightly sad or serious way
trick: PENSIVE ~ French 'penser' (to think): a thinking, quiet mood.
examples: She sucked her thumb and watched Rasheed in a sullen, pensive way.
He sat by the window in a pensive mood.

meaning: Just large or clear enough to be noticed
trick: PERCEPT-IBLE = able to be PERCEIVED.
examples: It was subtle but perceptible, and stronger with words that began with t.
There was a barely perceptible change in her voice.

usage.pattern: be perceptible (to someone) / a perceptible + noun

meaning: To sit on something high or narrow, like a bird on a branch; also a bar or branch where a bird rests
trick: A bird PERCHes on a branch like a PERSON on a high CHair.
examples: He would perch on a stump, flap his black wings, and talk for hours.
The kids like to perch on the wall and watch the cricket.

meaning: Sitting or resting on top or at the edge of something high or narrow
trick: PERCHED = like a bird sitting on its PERCH.
examples: At night his glasses were perched on the tip of his nose.
A small bird perched on the window and sang.

usage.pattern: perched on something / be perched on something

meaning: Bars or branches where birds sit and rest
trick: PERCHES: the bars a bird PERCHES on.
examples: The birds jumped on to their perches, and the whole farm was asleep in a moment.
The parrot moved between two perches in its cage.

meaning: Having a row or set of small holes punched through it
trick: PER-FOR-ATED: punched through (PER) FOR a tear line.
examples: He held the perforated end of the brown leather belt.
Tear the page along the perforated line.

meaning: Done only as a duty, quickly and without real care or interest
trick: PERFUNCTORY = PERFORM only like a FACTORY routine, no heart in it.
examples: It came out sounding perfunctory, like the token comfort of a kind stranger.
He gave a perfunctory nod and walked away.

meaning: (of vision) seen at the side, not straight ahead; also less important, at the edge
trick: PERIPHERAL = on the PERIPHERY (edge) of what you see.
examples: Stars gathered in my peripheral vision.
I saw the car out of my peripheral vision.

usage.pattern: peripheral + noun / be peripheral to something

meaning: The outer edge or boundary of an area
trick: PERI (around) + phery: the line that goes AROUND an area, like a PERImeter.
examples: She walked around the west-facing periphery of the clearing.
Small shops stand on the periphery of the city.

meaning: A long tube with mirrors that lets you see over things, used in submarines
trick: PERI (around) + SCOPE (look): look around from below the water.
examples: A hand came up, like a submarine periscope breaking the surface.
The captain looked through the periscope at the ship.

meaning: Died, especially in a war, accident or disaster; also (of things) rotted or decayed
trick: PERISHED: they PERISHed and were gone, like PERISHable food.
examples: She was going back to the land where her parents and brothers perished.
Many people perished in the flood.

meaning: Dying or being destroyed; also (British, informal) very cold
trick: PERISHING ~ PERISHable: things that are going bad and fading.
examples: She would grab whatever she could—a look, a whisper—to save it from perishing.
Help came too late to stop the crops from perishing.

meaning: Spread through every part of something (a smell, liquid or feeling)
trick: PER (through) + MEAT-ed: the smell went through the whole meat.
examples: The stench permeated the camp and their own bodies.
The smell of fresh bread permeated the house.

meaning: Spreads through every part of something
trick: PERMEATES: goes PER (through) every part, like water through a sponge.
examples: Pain permeates each cell in your body, begging you to stop.
The smell of coffee permeates the whole office.

meaning: The quality of standing straight up at a right angle to the ground
trick: PERPENDICULAR + ITY: the 'being upright' of a wall.
examples: The animals admired the strength and perpendicularity of its walls.
The builder checked the perpendicularity of the pillar with a string.

meaning: Never ending or changing; happening all the time
trick: PERPETUAL ~ PERMANENT + continual: it goes on forever.
examples: For several months now, the perpetual scowl had cleared from her brow.
Our street has a perpetual traffic problem.

usage.pattern: a perpetual + noun / in a perpetual state of something

meaning: All the time; in a way that never stops
trick: PERPETUAL + LY: always, forever.
examples: Some people perpetually feel that they are unworthy of the world.
He is perpetually late for meetings.

meaning: To make something bad continue for a long time
trick: PERPETUATE = make PERPETUAL (keep it going forever).
examples: To deny that negativity is to perpetuate problems rather than solve them.
Jokes like that perpetuate old stereotypes.

meaning: Confused because you cannot understand something
trick: PERPLEXED: the problem is too COMPLEX, so you're PERPLEXED.
examples: Readers came to me perplexed by questions like 'How do I apply for a job?'
She looked perplexed by the strange message.

meaning: Confusing and hard to understand
trick: PERPLEXING = COMPLEX-ing: it makes your head spin.
examples: His worries were both perplexing and thrilling.
The instructions were perplexing, so I called for help.

meaning: Continuing to try hard even when things are difficult
trick: PER-SEVERE-ANCE: keep going through SEVERE times.
examples: Suffering through your fears is what lets you build courage and perseverance.
With perseverance, she finally passed the exam.

meaning: To keep trying to do something even though it is difficult
trick: PER-SEVERE: keep going even when it gets SEVERE.
examples: If you manage those moments of pain, you will be in a better position to persevere.
If you persevere, your English will get better.

meaning: The people who work for an organization or the army
trick: PERSONNEL = PERSONs on the team (double N for many people).
examples: Back in 2007, we lacked the personnel to get it done.
Only medical personnel are allowed in this room.

meaning: Sweat; the water that comes out of your skin when you are hot
trick: PER (through) + SPIRE (breathe): the skin 'breathes out' water.
examples: Beads of perspiration glistened on his forehead.
After the run, his shirt was wet with perspiration.

meaning: To sweat
trick: PERSPIRE = PERSPIRATION as a verb: you sweat.
examples: If you go too fast, you perspire, and the cold air in the church gives you a chill.
I perspire a lot in the summer heat.

meaning: Good at making people believe or do something
trick: PERSUASIVE: good at PERSUADING.
examples: When he argued a hard point, he had a way of whisking his tail that was very persuasive.
She gave a persuasive speech about saving water.

meaning: Worried or upset about something
trick: PER-TURB-ED ~ TURBulence: your mind is shaken.
examples: The lawyer interrupted me, looking greatly perturbed.
She was perturbed by the strange noise at night.

meaning: Spreading through every part of something
trick: PERVADE ~ PER (through) + 'wade': wading through every part.
examples: Snowball seemed like an invisible influence, pervading the air about them.
A smell of smoke was pervading the whole building.

meaning: The quality of being present everywhere
trick: PERVASIVE + NESS: the 'everywhere-ness' of something.
examples: The pervasiveness of technology is messing up people's expectations of themselves.
The pervasiveness of mobile phones has changed how we talk.

meaning: Strange and unreasonable, often doing or feeling the opposite of what is expected
trick: PERVERSE = PER + VERSE: turned the wrong way.
examples: I remember feeling a perverse pride in showing my fake grades to my mother.
He takes a perverse pleasure in making people wait.

meaning: Behaviour that is strange, wrong or unnatural; also the wish to do the opposite of what is reasonable
trick: PERVERSITY = being PERVERSE: twisted the wrong way.
examples: She was afraid of what she saw as acts of perversity.
Out of sheer perversity, he did the opposite of what he was told.

usage.pattern: out of (sheer) perversity / an act of perversity

meaning: An annoying person or thing; also an insect or animal that damages crops or homes
trick: PEST = PESTer: it keeps annoying you.
examples: Hearing it still made her feel like she was a pest, a cockroach.
My little brother is a pest when I'm studying.

meaning: To keep asking someone for something in an annoying way
trick: PESTER: be a PEST.
examples: Laila had to pester him in order to get a few more minutes with Aziza.
The kids pester me for ice cream every evening.

usage.pattern: pester someone for something / to do something

meaning: Annoying someone by asking for something again and again
trick: PESTERING: acting like a PEST.
examples: Then stop pestering me!
He kept pestering his father for a new bike.

usage.pattern: pestering someone for something / to do something

meaning: (of a woman) small and slim in an attractive way
trick: PETITE = French 'small' (like 'petty').
examples: Short and petite, Sister Katherine was sixty years old.
The dress comes in a petite size.

meaning: Extremely frightened, so much that you cannot move; also turned into stone
trick: PETR = stone: so scared you turn to stone.
examples: The thought of thirty-five more miles petrified me.
She was petrified of the dark as a child.

usage.pattern: something petrified someone / be petrified of something

meaning: Small and not important; also caring too much about small things in an unkind way
trick: PETTY ~ French 'petit' (small).
examples: After the war they were unfazed by life's petty annoyances.
Let's not fight over petty things.

meaning: Felt or seen but not real; also a ghost
trick: PHANTOM ~ FANTASY: it feels real but isn't.
examples: The ache of his absence was like the phantom pain of an amputee.
My phone often gives me phantom buzzes in my pocket.

meaning: Extremely good or great; very unusual
trick: PHENOMENAL = like a rare PHENOMENON.
examples: The warm Hawaiian sun felt phenomenal, and I got the job done.
She has a phenomenal memory for names.

meaning: Something that happens or exists, especially something unusual or interesting
trick: PHENOMENON = something that FEN-OMENally shows itself.
examples: There's a phenomenon that happens when one muscle group is worked too hard.
A rainbow is a natural phenomenon.

meaning: Thick sticky liquid from the throat or nose, especially when you are ill
trick: PHLEGM: silent PH and G, like the gunk stuck silently in your throat.
examples: Whenever he spat out the window, his phlegm flew back into my face.
A cold leaves my throat full of phlegm.

meaning: Glowing softly in the dark
trick: PHOSPHOR (light-bringer) + escent: glows like phosphorus.
examples: She could see their wings catching the phosphorescent blue of moonlight.
The waves were phosphorescent at night.

meaning: Heavy tools with a long handle and a curved iron head, used for breaking hard ground or rock
trick: PICK + AXE: an axe that picks at stone.
examples: Men wielding pickaxes smashed statues in the old Kabul Museum.
The workers broke the rocks with pickaxes.

meaning: Touched or pulled at something again and again with the fingers, often from nerves; also ate only a little of food
hindi: नोचती रही, कुरेदती रही; थोड़ा-थोड़ा खाया
trick: PICK AT = keep PICKING little bits.
examples: She picked at her hair and bit the mole below her lip.
He was not hungry and just picked at his food.

meaning: (of food) kept in vinegar or salt water so it lasts and tastes sour
trick: PICKLED = made into a PICKLE.
examples: He took a pinch of the pickled eggplant Mariam had made that summer.
Grandma makes pickled mango every summer.

meaning: (of an animal) having patches of two colours, usually black and white
trick: PIE + BALD: patchy like a magpie (pie) with bald spots.
examples: The young pigs were piebald.
The farmer rode a piebald horse.

meaning: A long platform built out over the sea where boats stop or people walk
trick: PIER: you PEER out at the sea from the PIER.
examples: The race started from the beach beside the pier in downtown Kona.
We walked to the end of the pier to watch the sunset.

meaning: Strong religious belief and practice
trick: PIETY ~ PIOUS: religious and devoted.
examples: Wajma raised a finger, her voice shaking with piety.
He was known for his piety and kindness.

usage.pattern: with piety / an act of piety

meaning: Raw iron straight from a furnace, before it is made into steel
trick: PIG-IRON: hot iron poured into moulds shaped like piglets around a sow.
examples: A voice read out figures about the production of pig-iron.
The factory turns pig-iron into steel.

meaning: Grey birds often seen in cities; in the old days some carried messages
trick: PIGEON: the city bird you see PIGging on bread crumbs.
examples: They must send out more and more pigeons and stir up rebellion on other farms.
Old men sit in the park and feed the pigeons.

meaning: Farm animals with a flat snout and a curly tail, kept for meat
trick: PIGS: oink, oink!
examples: First came the three dogs, and then the pigs, who settled in the straw.
The farmer feeds the pigs every morning.

meaning: People who travel to a holy place for religious reasons
trick: PILGRIMS take a PIL-GRIM (long, hard) journey to a holy place.
examples: The caves were a shelter for weary travelling pilgrims.
Thousands of pilgrims visit the temple every year.

meaning: Collecting in a growing heap; also putting things on top of each other
trick: PILING = making a PILE.
examples: Snow was piling in heaps on sidewalks and roofs.
Dirty dishes kept piling up in the sink.

usage.pattern: something piling (up) / piling something on something

meaning: To steal things violently from a place, especially in a war
trick: PILLAGE: they take the PILE from the vILLAGE.
examples: These fighters went on to fight and pillage as before.
The army would pillage every village it passed.

meaning: A man who controls prostitutes and takes the money they earn
trick: PIMP = a man who PIMPs (sells) others for profit.
examples: The general idea around here is that he's a pimp.
The police arrested a pimp in the old city.

meaning: Covered with pimples (small red spots on the skin)
trick: PIMPLY = full of PIMPLES.
examples: Under a big pimply nose, his lips were trembling.
He was a shy, pimply teenager.

meaning: A small amount of something held between finger and thumb; also to squeeze skin hard with finger and thumb
trick: PINCH = the amount between your two fingertips.
examples: He took a pinch of the pickled eggplant.
Add a pinch of salt to the soup.

meaning: A small soft pad for sticking pins into when not in use
trick: PIN + CUSHION: a cushion for pins.
examples: His hair stood on his scalp like needles in a pincushion.
My mother keeps her needles in a red pincushion.

meaning: A tall evergreen tree with needle-like leaves; also to miss someone very much
trick: PINE: think of PINEapple and pine cones.
examples: The road finds shade in gathering stands of cedar and pine.
We sat under a tall pine in the hills.

usage.pattern: pine + noun / a stand of pine

meaning: The highest or best point of something
trick: PINNACLE ~ a PIN's point: the very top.
examples: I had always seen the marathon as the pinnacle of endurance racing.
Winning the World Cup was the pinnacle of his career.

meaning: (~ dream) a hope or plan that can never come true; also a tube for carrying water or gas
trick: PIPE DREAM: a dream from smoking a pipe, not from real life.
examples: What a pipe dream.
Owning a house in Mumbai feels like a pipe dream to me.

meaning: A small green nut; also a light green colour
trick: PISTACHIO: say 'pista' in Hindi — same nut!
examples: The living room had a pistachio green leather couch.
She sprinkled pistachio on top of the kheer.

meaning: A large deep hole in the ground; also (the ~ of the stomach) the deep inside of the belly
trick: PIT: you fall in and can't get out.
examples: The pit was filled with cold mud and topped off with icy water.
The workers dug a deep pit for the tank.

usage.pattern: in a pit / the pit of your stomach

meaning: A strong, muscular breed of dog, originally bred for fighting
trick: PIT BULL: a dog as strong as a BULL from the fighting PIT.
examples: Whatever you chose—keeping it, ignoring it, feeding it to a pit bull—there would be problems.
Our neighbour's pit bull is gentle with children.

meaning: A large jug for pouring water or other drinks
trick: PITCHER: you PITCH water into glasses from it.
examples: In the centre of the table was a vase of marigolds and a sweating pitcher of water.
Please fill the pitcher with cold water.

meaning: Falls or moves suddenly forward or backward; also throws a ball
hindi: गिरता है, झटके से झुकता है
trick: PITCHES: thrown forward like a PITCHED ball.
examples: She gasps, and her body pitches forward.
The boat pitches up and down in the storm.

meaning: (~ in) joining in to help with something; also throwing a ball
trick: PITCH IN = throw your effort IN with others.
examples: It was Laila's turn now, with Mariam pitching in, to fill the quiet with chatter.
Everyone was pitching in to clean the house before Diwali.

meaning: Hidden problems or dangers that are easy to fall into
trick: PITFALLS: PITs you FALL into without seeing them.
examples: I read blogs from runners who completed it and noted their pitfalls.
Every new business has its pitfalls.

meaning: Deserving pity; making you feel sorry for someone
trick: PITIABLE = able to make you feel PITY.
examples: To Laila, Tariq's mother never looked pitiable in it.
The stray dog was in a pitiable state.

meaning: In a way that makes you feel sorry for someone
trick: PITIABLY: in a PITY-making way.
examples: He looked vulnerable, pitiably confused, almost harmless.
The puppy cried pitiably in the rain.

meaning: Marked with small holes or scars on the surface; also (of fruit) with the stone removed
trick: PITTED: covered in little PITS.
examples: His nose was pocked with the same crater-like scars that pitted his cheeks.
The old road was pitted with holes after the rain.

usage.pattern: something pitted something / be pitted with something

meaning: In a way that shows you feel sorry for someone
trick: PITYINGLY = with PITY.
examples: How tired their arms and legs must be, she thought pityingly.
The teacher smiled pityingly at the nervous boy.

meaning: To cause continual trouble or suffering to someone; also a deadly disease that spreads fast
trick: PLAGUE: troubles that spread like a PLAGUE.
examples: It's these problems that plague us now.
Power cuts plague our town every summer.

meaning: Caused continual trouble or worry
trick: PLAGUED: as if hit by a PLAGUE of troubles.
examples: For a long time I was plagued by doubts about my future.
The team has been plagued by injuries this season.

meaning: Sounding sad and mournful
trick: PLAINTIVE ~ COMPLAINT: a sad, complaining sound.
examples: She heard the plaintive squeak of the cane seat when he sat.
The puppy gave a plaintive cry at the door.

meaning: (of hair) twisted together in strands; braided
trick: PLAITED sounds like 'plated': hair laid in a neat PLAT-TERn.
examples: She tossed her white mane, plaited with red ribbons.
Her hair was plaited for school.

meaning: Lengths of hair twisted together; braids
trick: PLAITS sounds like 'plates': two neat braids side by side.
examples: Laila's slim fingers tightened her plaits.
The little girl wore her hair in two plaits.

meaning: A flat metal or stone panel fixed to a wall; also a sticky layer on teeth
trick: PLAQUE: a PLAQUE on the wall, a PLAQUE on your teeth — both flat layers.
examples: The voice came from an oblong metal plaque on the right-hand wall.
A brass plaque on the door shows the doctor's name.

meaning: To stop rising or improving and stay at the same level; also a flat high area of land
trick: PLATEAU: like a flat PLATE — no more going up.
examples: I had so much weight to lose that I could not afford to plateau.
My running speed seems to plateau after a few weeks.

meaning: Covered with a thin layer of metal
trick: PLATED = covered with a metal PLATE.
examples: My thighs would need to be plated in steel.
She wore a gold-plated ring.

meaning: A small group of soldiers, usually led by a lieutenant
trick: PLATOON ~ PLATE-full of soldiers: a small team.
examples: After training, I landed in my first platoon.
The platoon marched through the village.

usage.pattern: in a platoon / lead a platoon

meaning: A large flat dish for serving food
trick: PLATTER = a big PLATE.
examples: A little boy ran toward our bus carrying a platter of cookies.
She brought out a platter of samosas for the guests.

meaning: Seeming reasonable and likely to be true
trick: PLAUSIBLE: you could APPLAUD it — sounds right.
examples: In one way it sounded unlikely; in another, it was plausible enough.
His excuse sounded plausible, so the teacher believed him.

meaning: Light-hearted and teasing, not serious; also full of fun
trick: PLAY + FUL: full of play.
examples: Laila was irritated by this roundabout, playful accusation.
The puppy is very playful in the morning.

meaning: A strong, emotional request for help or mercy; also a formal answer of guilty or not guilty in court
trick: PLEA ~ PLEASE: a plea is a big 'please!'
examples: Through a mouthful of grit and pebbles, Mariam mumbled a plea.
The child made a plea for one more story before bed.

usage.pattern: make a plea for something / a plea to someone

meaning: In a way that begs or asks desperately for something
trick: PLEAD + -INGLY: said the way a pleading person talks.
examples: "Surely, comrades," cried Squealer almost pleadingly, "surely no one wants to see Jones come back?"
The puppy looked at me pleadingly for a biscuit.

meaning: Having many narrow folds pressed or sewn into the cloth
trick: PLEATED = PLEAT + ED: folded neatly like an accordion.
examples: The yards of pleated cloth spilled over his knees when he lifted it.
She wore a pleated skirt to the party.

meaning: Existing in large amounts; more than enough
trick: PLENTY + FUL: full of plenty.
examples: After the sale of the hay, the stores of food for winter were none too plentiful.
Mangoes are plentiful in the summer.

usage.pattern: be plentiful / a plentiful supply of something

meaning: A hand tool with two hinged arms for gripping, bending or cutting wire
trick: PLIERS help you PLY (bend) wire.
examples: I thought I'd have to use a pair of pliers.
Dad used pliers to pull the nail out.

usage.pattern: a pair of pliers / use pliers to do something

meaning: To walk slowly with heavy steps; also to work slowly and steadily at a dull task
hindi: भारी कदमों से चलना, घिसटना; धीरे-धीरे मेहनत करना
trick: PLOD sounds like heavy boots: plod, plod, plod.
examples: The animals were glad to plod to and fro all day with blocks of stone.
We had to plod through the mud to reach the bus stop.

meaning: Walked slowly with heavy, tired steps
hindi: भारी कदमों से चला, घिसटते हुए गया
trick: PLOD + DED: plod-plod-plodded along.
examples: I plodded over to a grassy slope in the woods and lay back on the pine needles.
After the long hike, we plodded back to the car.

meaning: A person who works slowly and steadily but without special talent or speed
trick: PLODDER = one who PLODS along, never sprinting.
examples: Back then, I was a plodder.
He was a plodder at school, but he never gave up.

usage.pattern: be a plodder / a steady plodder

meaning: Walking slowly with heavy, tired steps; also slow and dull
hindi: भारी कदमों से चलता हुआ; धीमा, नीरस
trick: PLOD + DING: still plodding, step after heavy step.
examples: For a few miles I could see him plodding in the distance through the lava fields.
The old horse kept plodding up the hill.

meaning: Gaps or mistakes in a story that make it not make sense
hindi: कहानी की कमियाँ, कथानक की खामियाँ
trick: PLOT HOLES = HOLES in the story's PLOT.
examples: We fill in a couple of the plot holes with our own details so the story makes sense.
The movie was fun, but it had too many plot holes.

usage.pattern: plot holes in something / fill (in) the plot holes

meaning: A large farm tool pulled by animals or a tractor to turn over soil; also to dig soil with this (US: plow)
trick: PLOUGH (British) = PLOW (US): it ploughs the ground.
examples: He is too weak to pull the plough.
The farmer tied the ox to the plough.

usage.pattern: pull a plough / plough a field

meaning: Cleared of snow with a plow (US spelling); also dug with a plow
trick: PLOWED = the snowPLOW has been through.
examples: Those trails were never plowed.
The roads were plowed early in the morning.

meaning: Pushing snow away to clear it (US spelling); also digging soil with a plow
hindi: बर्फ़ हटाते हुए; हल चलाते हुए
trick: PLOWING = PLOW at work, pushing snow or soil.
examples: Mariam watched the merchants plowing snow from their storefronts.
Trucks were plowing the streets all night.

usage.pattern: plow something / plow snow from something

meaning: A clever plan or trick used to gain an advantage
trick: PLOY rhymes with TOY: a trick you play with.
examples: It was a ploy I used to keep my mental edge and help our crew prevail.
His sad story was just a ploy to get money.

usage.pattern: a ploy to do something / a clever ploy

meaning: (Of hair) pulled out to shape it; also picked or pulled off quickly
trick: PLUCKED: like PLUCKING a chicken's feathers, hair pulled out.
examples: Mariam took in their plucked eyebrows and thin, tolerant smiles.
She plucked a flower from the garden.

usage.pattern: plucked + noun / pluck something from something

meaning: Pulling out hairs to shape them; also picking or pulling something off
trick: PLUCKING: pulling one hair (or string) at a time.
examples: "You're plucking your eyebrows," Mammy said.
He sat on the steps, plucking the strings of his guitar.

usage.pattern: pluck something / pluck something from something

meaning: Long clouds of smoke, steam or dust rising into the air; also large feathers
trick: PLUMES = long feathery shapes, like smoke feathers in the sky.
examples: In the distance, sudden plumes of smoke rose to the sky.
Plumes of steam rose from the hot tea.

meaning: To fall very fast from a height; also to drop suddenly in value
hindi: तेज़ी से गिरना, धड़ाम से गिरना
trick: PLUMMET ~ PLUMB (a lead weight) dropping straight down.
examples: Your voice reminds you that you're not about to plummet to your death.
Prices plummet after the festival season.

meaning: Pleasantly full and round (of fruit); also slightly fat (of a person)
trick: PLUMP = PLUM-shaped: round and full.
examples: He described the vines heavy with plump grapes.
The baby had plump little cheeks.

meaning: A sudden dive or jump straight into something; also to fall or push suddenly downward
trick: PLUNGE: the plunger dives straight into the water.
examples: The novel opens with a cold plunge straight into a grim April day.
He took a quick plunge into the cold lake.

usage.pattern: a plunge into something / take the plunge

meaning: Put someone suddenly into a bad situation; also fell or dived suddenly
trick: PLUNGED: dropped straight in, like a stone into water.
examples: Each stretch plunged me into the fire.
The power cut plunged the town into darkness.

meaning: Expensive, comfortable and luxurious; also a soft, thick fabric
trick: PLUSH = PLUS comfort: everything extra soft and rich.
examples: I was in a plush hotel room in Vegas when I got the call.
They sat on a plush red sofa.

meaning: A serious infection that fills the lungs with fluid and makes breathing hard
trick: PNEUMONIA: silent P, like PNEU = air/lungs (pneumatic).
examples: I was pulled out on a medical after getting double pneumonia.
Grandpa was in hospital with pneumonia last winter.

meaning: Covered with small holes, pits or marks
trick: POCKED = full of little POCKETS (pits).
examples: Pete stomped the pocked asphalt, his brow slick with sweat.
The old wall was pocked with bullet holes.

usage.pattern: pocked + noun / be pocked with something

meaning: Held still in position, ready to move or act; also calm and confident
trick: POISED = in a POSE, held still and ready.
examples: The coachman's glossy black hat seemed poised above the hearse.
The cat sat poised to jump on the mouse.

usage.pattern: be poised above something / be poised to do something

meaning: A wild plant (pokeweed) with poisonous roots; used to mean an unwanted, worthless weed
trick: POKEROOT: a weed whose ROOT pokes up where nobody wants it.
examples: To Jalil and his wives, I was a pokeroot.
The farmer pulled the pokeroot out of his field.

meaning: Pushing something into or against someone with a finger or pointed thing
trick: POKING: like poking a fire with a stick.
examples: "You couldn't stretch a leg here without poking a poet," he laughed.
Stop poking your brother with that pencil!

meaning: The official group of people whose job is to keep order and catch criminals
trick: POLICE keep POLICY (rules) in the city (Greek polis).
examples: His last companion was killed in a shootout with the local police.
We called the police when we saw the break-in.

usage.pattern: call the police / the police + verb (plural)

meaning: A pattern of round dots spaced evenly on cloth (usually spelled polka dot)
trick: POLKA DOT: dots dancing a POLKA across the cloth.
examples: Man, woman, black, white, or purple polkadot, it doesn't matter.
She wore a red dress with white polkadots.

meaning: A round red fruit with a thick skin full of juicy red seeds
trick: POMEGRANATE = POME (apple) + GRANATE (many grains/seeds).
examples: There is a pomegranate tree in the yard and a thicket of sweetbriar bushes.
I had a glass of pomegranate juice for breakfast.

meaning: A loose blanket-like cloak with a hole in the middle for the head
trick: PONCHO = a blanket with a hole: pop your head through.
examples: Kate placed a camouflaged poncho liner over my body as I shivered.
He pulled on a plastic poncho when the rain started.

usage.pattern: wear a poncho / a rain poncho

meaning: To think carefully about something for some time
trick: PONDER = sit by a POND and think.
examples: It did not occur to young Mariam to ponder the unfairness of it.
She paused to ponder the question.

meaning: Small openings in a hen-house that let hens go in and out
trick: POPHOLES = holes hens POP in and out of.
examples: Jones locked the hen-houses but was too drunk to shut the popholes.
Grandma closed the popholes so the fox couldn't get in.

meaning: A tall, thin, fast-growing tree with soft wood
trick: POPLAR: POPular tree that shoots up tall and thin.
examples: "I'll wait here," he says, sitting on a rock beneath a poplar.
A row of poplar trees lined the road.

meaning: Tall, thin, fast-growing trees with soft wood
trick: POPLARS: a row of tall thin trees, popping up.
examples: The track led to a flat field where poplars and cottonwoods soared.
Poplars swayed in the wind along the river.

meaning: A hard, fine, shiny white ceramic used for cups, plates and ornaments
trick: PORCELAIN: so fine and shiny you won't PAWS on it.
examples: Nana cherished each blue-and-white porcelain piece.
She keeps her grandmother's porcelain cups in a glass cabinet.

meaning: A covered area in front of the entrance of a house
trick: PORCH: where you PERCH before you enter.
examples: Four square pillars framed a front porch that led to the widest lawn.
We sat on the porch and drank tea.

usage.pattern: on the porch / a front/back porch

meaning: Young pigs, especially ones raised for meat
trick: PORKERS = pigs that become PORK.
examples: You young porkers sitting in front of me will scream your lives out within a year.
The farmer fed the porkers twice a day.

meaning: Not firm or clear, letting things pass through easily; also full of tiny holes that let water or air through
trick: POROUS = full of PORES, so things leak through.
examples: In a toxic relationship, there will be a poor and porous sense of responsibility.
Sponges are porous, so they soak up water.

meaning: A soft food made by boiling oats or other grain in milk or water
trick: PORRIDGE: POUR the milk into the oats.
examples: She made a pot of brown porridge.
I eat warm porridge with honey every morning.

usage.pattern: a bowl of porridge / make porridge

meaning: Things that you own
trick: POSSESSIONS = what you POSSESS.
examples: In 2009, I gathered up all my possessions, sold them or put them into storage.
He lost all his possessions in the fire.

meaning: Relating to the post or mail service
trick: POSTAL = by POST: stamps and letters.
examples: He opened a branch in Paris to deal with companies without postal delays.
The postal service is closed on Sundays.

meaning: (with 'child') a person seen as the perfect example of something; also a large printed picture or notice put on a wall
trick: POSTER child: your face on the POSTER for the cause.
examples: I was the poster child of that term we've all heard before: "at-risk youth."
A movie poster hung on her bedroom wall.

usage.pattern: the poster child for/of something / put up a poster

meaning: A chemical element; a mineral the body needs, found in bananas and other fruit
trick: POTASSIUM: K on the table, found in a banana's POT.
examples: I didn't even consider my potassium levels or eat any fresh fruit.
Bananas are a good source of potassium.

meaning: Great power or strength to affect people or things
trick: POTENCY = being POTENT: full of power.
examples: The words packed a fierce potency, and she unleashed them now.
The medicine loses its potency after a year.

usage.pattern: the potency of something / have potency

meaning: Very powerful or effective
trick: POTENT ~ POTENTial: lots of power stored inside.
examples: If you find your edge in the person standing in your way, that's potent.
This is a potent medicine, so take only one tablet.

meaning: A deep hole in the surface of a road
trick: POTHOLE = a hole as deep as a POT in the road.
examples: She feared breaking an ankle stepping into a pothole.
The car hit a pothole and got a flat tyre.

meaning: A drink of medicine, poison or magic liquid
trick: POTION = a magic POT of drink.
examples: The girl drinks a potion that will put her to sleep for two days.
The witch mixed a love potion in her pot.

usage.pattern: drink/take a potion / a potion that does something

I use a pumice stone to soften my rough feet.

meaning: Hitting someone or something again and again with the fists (US spelling)
trick: PUMMELING = PUMMEL like a drum, beat after beat.
examples: The boxer kept pummeling the punching bag.
Heavy rain was pummeling the roof all night.

meaning: Stressed or broke up words or events with something at intervals
hindi: बीच-बीच में ज़ोर दिया, बीच-बीच में रोका
trick: PUNCTUATED = adding PUNCTUATION marks to your speech.
examples: He punctuated his words by pointing with his finger.
Her speech was punctuated by loud cheers.

usage.pattern: punctuate something with something / be punctuated by something

meaning: A place or situation of suffering or waiting that seems endless
trick: PURGATORY = where you are PURGED (cleaned) by suffering.
examples: The cost of quitting would be lifelong purgatory.
Waiting in the hospital for news was pure purgatory.

meaning: Made the low, soft sound a happy cat makes; also spoke in a soft, pleased voice
trick: PURRED = the cat's 'purrr' sound.
examples: The cat purred contentedly throughout Major's speech.
The kitten purred on my lap.

meaning: Pressed the lips together tightly into a small round shape
trick: PURSED lips = closed tight like a PURSE.
examples: Rasheed pursed his lips and blew, then put the spoon into his mouth.
She pursed her lips when she disagreed.

meaning: The act of carrying out a plan or aim (formal); "in ... of" = while trying to achieve or carry out
trick: PURSUANCE = PURSUing something.
examples: He acted in pursuance of an old family quarrel.
The rules were changed in pursuance of the new law.

meaning: The act of trying to get or achieve something; also chasing someone
trick: PURSUIT = PURSUE it.
examples: Ask any drug addict how his pursuit of pleasure turned out.
He moved to Mumbai in pursuit of his dream.

usage.pattern: in pursuit of something / the pursuit of something

meaning: Suggested or offered an idea for others to consider; also (of plants) produced leaves or shoots
trick: PUT it FORTH = put it forward on the table.
examples: Miller put forth the idea that we can process about seven pieces of information.
She put forth a new plan at the meeting.

meaning: Rotting and smelling very bad
trick: PUTRID = PUTrefying - rotting.
examples: The putrid stink made our eyes water.
The fridge was full of putrid food.

meaning: Moved around doing small, unhurried jobs (US; British: pottered)
trick: PUTTERED = PUTTing things here and there, slowly.
examples: She puttered around the kitchen for a while.
Grandpa puttered in the garden all morning.

meaning: Piles or stacks shaped like a pyramid; also large stone tombs in Egypt
trick: PYRAMIDS = piles with a point on top, like Egypt's.
examples: Old vendors sat behind pyramids of cherries and mounds of grapes.
The shop stacked oranges in neat pyramids.
